_source.Study Protocol Description:
A set of 17 nonmetallic materials was collected from various teams at Marshall Space Flight Center for destructive bioburden analysis. While the ideal approach would include sterilization of material external surfaces, particularly if handled by operators, most of these materials were unable to undergo cleaning due to their tacky surfaces or porous nature. Therefore, no pre-cleaning of the specimens was employed. Instead, these data were viewed as worst-case experimental estimations and a proof-of-concept experiment to determine the feasibility of using metagenomics to evaluate microbial contamination associated with materials. To prepare for cryogrinding, the materials were first cut into cubes approximately 3 mm × 3 mm with clean scissors, according to the manufacturer’s specification. Using a SPEX 6875 Freezer/Mill and SPEX 6751 polycarbonate grinding vials (Cole Parmer, Vernon Hills, IL), samples were precooled for 10 minutes, cryoground for 3 cycles at 10 cycles per second (CPS) for 3 minutes each (a total of 9 minutes) until adequate grinding was observed. Ground material was collected in sterile pre-weighed tubes, then weighed to calculate the final material mass. A volume of 10–20 mL of sterile Tris-EDTA buffer was added and samples were vortexed for one minute.     To assess total culturable bioburden, three 250 uL aliquots of slurry were spread plated on tryptic soy agar (TSA) (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), using a sterile L-shaped spreader. To assess only the heat-tolerant population (e.g., spores), 1 mL of the slurry was heat-shocked at 80 C for ~20 minutes before spread-plating on TSA. The typical pour-plating method associated with the NSA was not employed in this study because of the material debris, sometimes quite dark, present in the samples which would occlude the observance of embedded colonies. Furthermore, the majority of the sample was preserved for DNA isolation and metagenomic analysis.
All plates were incubated at 32C for at least seven days. Colonies were examined throughout the seven day time course, and on the final day were photographed and representative colonies streaked for isolation. Once adequate growth was observed for pure colonies, the isolates were catalogued and a single colony was inoculated into 1.5–3 mL tryptic soy broth (TSB) and incubated at 32C. When turbid growth was observed, a 1:1 mixture of the culture and 25% glycerol was frozen at -80C.     Genomic DNA was extracted using the Zymo D6005 kit.     For PPS301, PPS302, PPS305, PPS307, PPS308, PPS309, PPS310, PPS312, PPS314, PPS316, and PPS323, the 16S rRNA gene was amplified, run on an agarose gel, purified, and then sent for sequencing at Azenta genewiz using the IDT 16S rRNA For primer (Catalog Number: 51-01-19-06). For PPS303, PPS304, PPS306, PPS313, PPS315, PPS317, and PPS324, the genomic DNA was sent directly to Azenta Genewiz for PCR and sequencing with proprietary primers in both forward and reverse directions.     Single-ended Sanger sequencing performed at Azenta Genewiz on a ABI 3730xl DNA Analyzer.     Material slurry was concentrated using 50K Amicon spin filters. Concentrated material was resuspended in Buffer ATL from a QIAamp UCP Pathogen Mini Kit (Qiagen) and split into triplicate. Samples were processed per the manufacturer’s instructions with the exception of the pre-lysis bead beating step which was omitted. The resulting DNA elution was then quantified using both a Nanodrop Lite (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and a Qubit fluorometer using High Sensitivity DNA quantification reagents (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA). The resulting samples were split into two sterile tubes. One set was quantified using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and the other set was analyzed using metagenomics. We also included a negative control where a blank tube was carried through the procedure alongside samples.     Sample DNA extracts and the blank were converted into dsDNA libraries using the NEBNext Ultra II library prep kit for Illumina and the NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina both from New England Biolabs (Ipswich, MA, USA). The libraries were simultaneously indexed and amplified with 18 PCR cycles, purified using AmPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter, Inc., Brea, CA, USA), and analyzed on an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 instrument using the high sensitivity DNA kit (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA).     Libraries were shotgun sequenced on a MiSeq FGx instrument with a v3, 600-cycle (2x300bp) cartridge.     Utilizing kraken2 v2.1.1, a human genome reference database was constructed from NCBI's RefSeq (GCF_000001405.39) GRCh38.p13, with --no-masking, and defaults of kmer-length 35 and minimizer-length of 31. FASTQ files were screened against this database, and all successfully classified reads were removed.     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12.     For further characterization using matrix assisted laser desorption/ionization time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), the 18 microbial isolates were shipped to collaborators at University of Illinois Chicago. Isolates were incubated on A1 agar medium for 4 days at ambient temperature. After incubation, a small volume of isolated colonies were transferred to a MALDI-TOF MS ground steel target plate (Bruker Daltonics, Billerica, MA, USA) using sterile toothpicks in biological replicates of 5. This was followed by 1 uL of 70% formic acid (7:3 Optima, Fisher Chemical: Optima LC-MS Grade Water Fisher Chemical) and 1 uL of α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid matrix (α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid powder [98% pure, Sigma-Aldrich, part C2020], 50% acetonitrile, 47.5% water, and 2.5% trifluoroacetic acid). Evaporation of the formic acid overlay was achieved prior to matrix application.     Protein MS data were then collected in positive linear mode on a rapifleX MALDI Tissuetyper mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) using the following parameters: 2000 shots; RepRate: 5000 Hz; delay: 28272 ns; ion source 1 voltage: 20 kV; ion source 2 voltage: 18.45 kV; lens voltage: 9 kV; mass range: 2 kDa to 19.99 kDa; matrix suppression cutoff: 1.6 kDa. Bruker Daltonics bacterial test standard (BTS) was used for external calibration.

_source.Study Publication Title: Identification of Bioburden Associated with Nonmetallic Spacecraft Materials Using Culture-Based and Metagenomic Analyses
_source.Study Description: As NASA continues its exploration of the solar system, additional considerations must be made for the design of these missions, considering the scientific goals they aim to achieve. There is a deep interest in life-detection missions on the Jovian moon Europa and Saturn’s moon Enceladus, both of which are thought to contain saltwater oceans under global ice shells. Life detection missions to these sensitive locations must adhere to NASA’s planetary protection requirements. These requirements include probabilistic analyses for contamination on the target body as well as limits on biological contamination (i.e., bioburden) on and in the spacecraft. Historically, NASA has relied heavily upon heat microbial reduction (HMR) to reduce bioburden embedded within nonmetallic materials used in spacecraft assemblies. However, given the long transit time expected for spacecraft aiming to reach Europa or Enceladus, there is additional risk that the harshness of the space environment coupled with HMR may adversely impact such materials. When a bioburden reduction method like HMR cannot be employed, NASA relies upon bioburden assumptions known as “specification values” to calculate bioburden. These values are known to be conservative, potentially inflating the true bioburden associated with materials. Therefore, there is an increased need for alternative bioburden evaluation methods for nonmetallic materials when HMR cannot be used. In this study, we compared the quantification approaches of culture-based methods with metagenomic analysis to evaluate the bioburden associated with 17 nonmetallic materials. We extracted DNA directly from nonmetallic materials and performed qPCR coupled with metagenomic sequencing. Isolated microbes from the culture-based assay were identified using a combination of 16S rRNA Sanger sequencing and MALDI-TOF MS. The results from this work demonstrate that while low biomass represents a challenge, metagenomics may be a feasible approach for supplementing culture-based methods for assessing bioburden. These findings lay a foundation for more advanced methods to evaluate material bioburden with greater specificity. Multiple methods of microbial identification also provide a framework to better inform planetary protection risks in deep space missions.

_source.Study Protocol Description: After 24 hours of cultivation, the contents of every bioreactor was gently mixed by pipetting and divided into several aliquots. Ten millilitres of culture from each growth condition was immediately fixed with RNA Protect Reagent (Qiagen), following the manufacturer's instructions, and fixed cell pellets were frozen at -20C until RNA extraction. Samples were immediately exposed to different stresses. The extraction of total RNA was performed with the Total RNA Isolation System (Promega). RNA quality and quantity were assessed using the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 electrophoresis system and the Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (NanoDrop technologies) respectively. cDNA synthesis and further processing for the transcriptomic analysis were performed according to the protocol of the GeneChip manufacturer (Affymetrix). Ten micrograms of total RNA per sample was used for cDNA synthesis and a Poly-A RNA control was added to the RNA sample using the GeneChip eukaryotic poly-A control kit (Affymetrix). The synthesis of cDNA was performed using denatured total RNA (70 C for 10 min), 13 ng/ul random hexamer primers (Roche), 0.5 U/ul SUPERase In (Ambion), 25 U/ul SuperScript II reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen), 0.5 nmol/ul deoxynucleoside triphosphates in 1x first strand buffer with 10 nmol/ul dithiothreitol. The latter mix was placed in a Thermocycler operated at 25 C for 10 min, 37 C for 60 min, 42 C for 60 min and 70 C for 10 min. The remaining RNA was degraded by treatment with 1 N NaOH, incubation for 30 min at 65 C and subsequent neutralization with 1 N HCl. cDNA was purified using a MiniElute PCR purification kit (Qiagen), where after the concentration of cDNA was assessed using the Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (NanoDrop technologies). Eight micrograms of cDNA was fragmented to a size range of 50-200 nucleotides with DNase I (Promega) for 10 min at 37 C where after the enzyme was inactivated at 99 C for 10 min. The fragmented cDNA was verified by loading a sample on a 2% agarose gel containing 0.1 %0  (v/v) GelRed (Biotium).     Fragmented cDNA was end-labelled with biotin-dUTP using the GeneChip DNA labelling reagent (Affymetrix) and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (Promega) in 1x reaction buffer  (Promega) at 37C for 60 min. The reaction was stopped using 0.5 M EDTA.     Biotinylated cDNA was hybridized to GeneChip P. aeruginosa Genome arrays (Affymetrix) by incubation in a GeneChip hybridization oven 640 at 50C with orbital shaking at 60 r.p.m. for 16 h in the following MES-buffer [2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid]: 0.1 ul herring sperm DNA (Promega), 0.5 ul bovine serum albumine (Invitrogen), 7.8% dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma-Aldrich), 50 mM B2 control oligo (Affymetrix) in 1x hybridization buffer (made according to instructions of Affymetrix GeneChip). Microarray slides were washed according to the manufacturer's protocol and stained using a fluidics station 450 (Affymetrix) and applying the Midi_euk2v3_450 protocol. Briefly, the staining procedure was comprised of the following steps: (i) binding of streptavidin (Invitrogen) to the biotin-labeled hybridized cDNA, (ii) binding of a biotin-conjugated streptavidin antibody (Labconsult) and (iii) binding of R-phycoerythrin-conjugated streptavidin (Invitrogen).     Microarrays were scanned at the emission wavelength of 570 nm where after the data analysis took place.     Raw Affymetrix data were pre-processed using the Affy package in BioConductor as follows: (i) background correction based on the robust multichip average (RMA) convolution model (Irizarry et al., 2003), (ii) quantile normalization to make expression values from different arrays more comparable (Bolstad et al., 2003), (iii) summarization of multiple probe intensities for each probe set to one expression value per gene using RMA (Irizarry et al., 2003). To test for differential expression between the different simulated microgravity (LSMMG and RG) conditions and the reference condition (NG) the Bayesian adjusted t-statistics was used as implemented in the LIMMA package (version 2.5.15) (Smyth, 2004). P-values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini and Hochber's method to control the false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Microarray analysis was performed on all three biological replicates.     Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7114 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/Microarray/Affymetrix/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7114_Versions/GL-DPPD-7114.md) using NF_MAAffymetrix version 1.0.5 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/tree/NF_MAAffymetrix_1.0.5/Microarray/Affymetrix/Workflow_Documentation/NF_MAAffymetrix). In short, a RunSheet containing raw data file location and processing metadata from the study's *ISA.zip file was generated using dp_tools (version 1.3.4). The raw array data files were loaded into R (version 4.1.3) using oligo (version 1.58.0). Raw data quality assurance density plot, pseudo images, MA plots, and boxplots were generated using oligo (version 1.58.0). The raw probe level intensity data was background corrected and normalized across arrays via the oligo (version 1.58.0) quantile method. Normalized probe level data quality assurance density plot, pseudo images, MA plots, and boxplots were generated using oligo (version 1.58.0). Normalized probe level data was summarized to the probeset level using the oligo (version 1.58.0) RMA method. Gene annotations were retrieved for each probeset from ThermoFisher (https://www.thermofisher.com/order/catalog/product/sec/assets?url=TFS-Assets/LSG/Support-Files/Pae_G1a-na36-annot-csv.zip, created March 2016, accessed June 2024). Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.1.3) using limma (version 3.50.3); all groups were compared pairwise for each probeset to generate a moderated t-statistic and associated p- and adjusted p-value.     The wild type P. aeruginosa PAO1 strain (ATCC 15692) was used in this study and all cultures were grown in Lennox L Broth Base (LB) (Life Technologies) at 28C. An overnight shaking culture (125 r.p.m.) of P. aeruginosa in LB was washed and diluted in 0.85% NaCl solution to an OD600 of 1. This bacterial suspension was used to inoculate fresh LB medium at a final concentration of 10-4 CFU/ml.     Synthecon Rotating Wall Vessel bioreactors (RWV) (50 ml or 10 ml) were filled with inoculated medium so that no headspace (i.e. no bubbles) was present. Other than for stress resistance assays, for which 10 ml capacity bioreactors were used, RWV bioreactors with a capacity of 50 ml were adopted for all experiments. Identical bioreactors were mounted in triplicate on (i) a RWV device in vertical position (LSMMG) (Cellon), (ii) a RWV device in horizontal position (NG) and (iii) the center of the inner Random Positioning Machine (RPM) frame (RG) (Fokker Space), and placed in a large humidified (70%-80% relative humidity) culture chamber, to avoid evaporation of culture medium through the gas-permeable membrane at the back of each vessel. A 25 r.p.m. rotation speed was adopted for the RWV cultures, while RPM-cultures were randomly rotated at 10 r.p.m. Bacteria were grown in the three described test conditions for 24 hours.

_source.Study Description: Anticipating the risk for infectious disease during space exploration and habitation is a critical factor to ensure safety, health and performance of the crewmembers. As a ubiquitous environmental organism that is occasionally part of the human flora, Pseudomonas aeruginosa could pose a health hazard for the immuno-compromised astronauts. In order to gain insights in the behavior of P. aeruginosa in spaceflight conditions, two spaceflight-analogue culture systems, i.e. the rotating wall vessel (RWV) and the random position machine (RPM), were used. Microarray analysis of P. aeruginosa PAO1 grown in the low shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG) environment of the RWV compared to the normal gravity control (NG), revealed a regulatory role for AlgU (RpoE). Specifically, P. aeruginosa cultured in LSMMG exhibited increased alginate production and up-regulation of AlgU-controlled transcripts, including those encoding stress-related proteins. This study also shows the involvement of Hfq in the LSMMG response, consistent with its previously identified role in the Salmonella LSMMG- and spaceflight response. Furthermore, cultivation in LSMMG increased heat and oxidative stress resistance and caused a decrease in the culture oxygen transfer rate. Interestingly, the global transcriptional response of P. aeruginosa grown in the RPM was similar to that in NG. The possible role of differences in fluid mixing between the RWV and RPM is discussed, with the overall collective data favoring the RWV as the optimal model to study the LSMMG-response of suspended cells. This study represents a first step towards the identification of specific virulence mechanisms of P. aeruginosa activated in response to spaceflight-analogue conditions, and could direct future research regarding the risk assessment and prevention of Pseudomonas infections for the crew in flight and the general public.

_source.Study Protocol Description: A cohort of 16-week-old female C57BL/6J mice were flown to the ISS, housed in the Rodent Habitat and were subjected to microgravity for 37 days. Mice of simiar age, sex and strain were used for ground controls housed in identical hardware and matching ISS environmental conditions. The mice were euthanized by ISS crew with Euthasol injection followed by cervical dislocation, frozen in a pre-chilled Mini Cold Bag (MCB) before transfer to the MELFI freezer (-80 C) and brought back to Earth. The study followed recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the protocol was approved by the NASA Flight Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).     The mouse carcasses were removed from -80 C storage and thawed at room temperature for 15-20 minutes. Multiple tissues, were collected from each carcass. Total dissection time for each carcass was no longer than 30 minutes since collection of the first tissue. After harvesting, right gastrocnemius muscle was stored separately overnight at 4 C in RNAlater, then transferred into a -80 C freezer.     RNA was extracted using the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD) following SOP  3.1-Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNa Mini with Qiagen RNase-Free DNase set. Homogenization buffer for RNA purification was made by adding 1:100 beta-mercaptoethanol to Buffer RLT (Qiagen, Germantown, MD) and kept on ice until use. Approximately 15-20 mg of tissue was weighed and immediately placed in 1.2 mL of the Buffer RLT solution. Tissue homogenization was performed using the Polytron Rotor Stator Homogenizer (Kinematica PT 1300 D) at 15 second intervals for a total of three intervals on an ice bath per the SOP  2.2-Tissue Homogenization using Polytron Rotor Stator Homogenizer. Homogenates were centrifuged for 5 minutes at RT and 14,000 g to remove cell debris. The supernatant from each sample was then used to isolate and purify RNA following the manufacturer protocol. RNA was eluted in 50 uL RNAse-free H2O. Concentration for all RNA samples were measured using Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) with Qubit RNA BR kit following SOP  4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with the Agilent RNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following SOP  6.3-QC cDNA. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     ERCC ExFold RNA Spike-In Mixes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat   4456739, v92), Mix 1 or Mix 2, were added on the day of library prep at the concentrations suggested by the manufacturer protocol.  Protocol followed is SOP  5.2 Use of ERCC Spike-In Mixes and UMRR/UHRR Controls for Total RNA Sequencing. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     All samples were normalized to an input of 10ng of total RNA and added to the UPX 3' Transcriptome kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD), following SOP  5.4-QIAseq UPX 3' Transcriptome Library Preparation.  Sample RINs greater than 8.5.  Cell IDs, which are used to distinguish individual samples, are added to each sample during the RT step.  This allows samples to be pooled together after the RT step and cary out library preparation on a pool of samples as opposed to individual samples.  An input of 50ng of pooled cDNA was used to carry out library construction.  Library fragment size for this pool of samples is ~540 bp and was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following protocol SOP  6.3-Quality Analysis of Sequencing Libraries Using 4200 TapeStation System with D1000 reagent kit.  Final library concentration and pooled library concentration were measured by qPCR with the QuantSudio 6 Flex Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), following SOP  6.7-Sequencing Library Quantification using QIAseq Library Quant Assay.  Library quality control was determined by iSeq100 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     RNA sequencing was performed by GeneLab Sample Processing Lab on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Asymmetric paired end (Read 1: 93bp, Index: 6pb, Read 2: 28bp).  PhiX included as control and to increase library diversity.  Protocol followed is SOP  7.1-Setting up NovaSeq 6000 and iSeq 100 Sequencers. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     RThe raw fastq file for each sample was assessed for % rRNA using HTStream SeqScreener (version 1.3.2) and raw fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate raw MultiQC reports.     Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.0.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/tree/NF_RCP_2.0.0/RNAseq/Workflow_Documentation/NF_RCP). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.5) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0), ERCC genes were removed, and the non-ERCC genes were normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1). Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.
_source.Study Description: In the NASA Rodent Research-1 (RR-1) validation study, ten 16-week-old female C57BL/6J mice were flown to the ISS for 37 days before euthanasia and subsequent dissection (Flight group). Due to crew time constraint, only two (out of ten) mice were dissected immediately after euthanasia to recover spleen and liver tissues on the ISS. The remaining eight animals were euthanized, then intact carcasses were placed in a pre-chilled cold stowage container and stored in the MELFI. There were respective cohorts of age-matched basal animals which were euthanized one day after launch as a baseline control (Basal control group) as well as age-matched ground control animals kept in an ISS Environmental Simulator at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on a 4-day delay to mimic spaceflight conditions (Ground control group). In addition, the NASA Validation study also had a cohort of age-matched vivarium control animals that were housed in the vivarium cages and followed the same experimental timeline and process as the spaceflight animals (Vivarium control group). This dataset was generated only from Flight (n of 4) and Ground control (n of 8) animals that were euthanized and preserved intact on-orbit for subsequent dissection on the ground. Libraries were generated using a 3’ Tag-seq approach and sequenced at a depth of 40 M clusters (SE 93 bp).

_source.Study Protocol Description:
Rodent Research Reference Mission 1 (RRR-1) / Rodent Research-8 (RR-8) consisted of 40 BALB/cAnNTac females (8 used for this study) termed Flight which were sent on 12/5/2018 to the International Space Station (ISS), and a control group of 40 mice remained on Earth, termed Habitat Ground Control (HC). Furthermore, two age groups were used, younger (∼3 months) and older (∼8 months). All mouse work was completed with approval of the NASA Flight Animal Care and Use Committee (Protocol  FLT-18-116). Mice were received following landing at Scripps Research Institute (09-0004, for animal receipt upon landing) and transported to Stanford University IACUC (WYS1591). Flight mice were housed at double density on launch and again during the return to earth. HC mice were housed to match, as closely as possible, conditions experienced by Flight mice. This included double density housing in identical Mouse Habitat Units and Transporters as used by NASA during launch for Flight mice, and matched temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide levels (elevated on the ISS compared to Earth) based on actual flight environmental monitoring. All mice were adapted to NASA Nutrient Food Bars, four weeks prior to launch, and bars were exchanged weekly. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. During the mission we encountered the following issues, altering the planned experimental design, or that must be considered upon interpretation of results. (1) Within 24h of the planned launch, mold was found on the food bars, affecting both Flight and HGC mice to an unknown degree. It is possible that the mice were able to eat around the mold. The late replacement of the food bars, now secured with double-sided tape instead of epoxy, caused the bars to free-float during launch and return. The bars of the HGC mice fell to the bottom of the cage. Although the Flight mice appeared healthy upon arrival to the ISS, this might have induced additional stress. Due to concerns about mold, as more was discovered aboard the ISS, the ISS Term mice were sacrificed after approximately 3 weeks of microgravity rather than the planned 8 weeks, and ground controls were sacrificed to match this new timeline.(2) Due to poor weather, the return of the Flight LAR mice was delayed and the mice spent 7 instead of the normal 2-3 days in double density housing. This housing is more confined (10 mice per cage side instead of the 5 in the normal habitat), video monitoring was not possible and food bars likely became unsecured and were free-floating. Conditions of the HGC mice were matched to these conditions, likely causing additional stress for both groups. Due to the weather, the Flight group likely experienced rough seas upon splashdown and shipping back to shore, which was not controlled for in the HGC group.     HC mice were shipped to Scripps Institute just prior to the return of the Flight mice so that all mice could be dissected together in matching conditions (+/- 1 day). The mice from the Flight group were returned alive to Earth on 1/14/2019 after 39.5 days on the ISS and collected 2-4 days after splashdown following functional assays at Scripps Research Institute. In this study, fresh organ samples were obtained and immediately processed from 8 live mice that arrived at Stanford University from Scripps Research Institute on 1/16/2019. Two mice each from the following groups were included: Flight 3mo, Flight 8mo, HC 3mo, HC 8mo. All four Flight mice were dissected on 1/16/2019 to minimize time spent outside of microgravity, and all four HC mice dissected on 1/17/2019. LAR mice were anesthetized with gas anesthesia and euthanized by means of cardiac
puncture blood draw (exsanguination) and double thoracotomy.     All the tissues were processed as previously described (https://doi.org:10.1038/s41586-020-2496-1). Isolated bones from forelimbs, hindlimbs, hips, and vertebrae were crushed in FACS buffer (2% sterile FBS in PBS) on ice, filtered through a 100 um strainer (Falcon 352360), pelleted (300 x g, 4C, 5 minutes), and resuspended in FACS buffer with 100 U/ml DNase I (Worthington LS006344) and 20 ug/ml Rat-IgG (Abcam ab37361) for 10 minutes on ice. Cells were incubated with anti-CD117 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec 130-091-224) on ice for 20 minutes, pelleted, resuspended in FACS buffer, and filtered through a 40 um strainer (Falcon 352340) into an LS column (Miltenyi Biotec 130-042-401). Following magnetic purification, c-Kit+ cells were eluted, and the flow through was depleted of RBCs with Histopaque-1119 (Sigma-Aldrich RNBF0417). The c-Kit+ cells and RBC-depleted flow through were resuspended in FACS buffer with Rat-IgG (20 ug/mL) and incubated on ice for 10 minutes. The flow-through was stained for B-cells, T-cells, and granulocytes. All antibodies were used at 1:50. c-Kit+ cells were stained with CD3-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone 17A2), Ly-6G/Ly-6C/GR1-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone RB6-8C5), CD11B/MAC1-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone M1/70), CD45R/B220-FITC (BioLegend 133301, clone RA3-6B2), TER119-FITC (BioLegend 133301), CKIT-APC (BioLegend 105812, clone 2B8), SCA-1-PECy7 (BioLegend 122514, clone E13-161.7). B-cells were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), B220-FITC (BioLegend 103206, clone RA3-6B2), IgM-PECy7 (BioLegend 406514, clone RMM-1). T-cells were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), CD90/Thy1.1-AF488 (BioLegend 202506, clone OX-7), CD90/Thy1.2-FITC (BioLegend 140304, clone 53-2.1), CD2-PECy7 (BioLegend 100114, clone RM2-5). Granulocytes were stained with TER119-PECy5 (BioLegend 116210), CD11B/MAC1-FITC (BioLegend 101206, clone M1/70), Ly-6G/Ly-6C/GR1-PECy7 (BioLegend 108416, clone RB6-8C5). Cells were incubated in antibody for 20 minutes, washed with FACS buffer, and pelleted (300 x g, 4C, 5 minutes). After resuspension in FACS buffer, cells were filtered into 35 um FACS tubes (Falcon 352235) and stained with 1:1000 SYTOX Blue (ThermoFisher S34857) immediately prior to sorting.     Cells were loaded in each channel with a target output of up to 5,000 cells per sample, though fewer cells were captured for small sample types. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed following the 10x Genomics protocol using the GemCode Single-Cell 3’ Gel Bead and Library v3 Kit. All reactions were performed in a Biorad C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with a 96-Deep Well Reaction Module. Twelve cycles were used for cDNA amplification and sample index PCR. Amplified cDNA and final libraries were evaluated on a Fragment Analyzer using a High Sensitivity NGS Analysis Kit (Advanced Analytical). Library preparation was performed one organ type at a time, in sets of eight samples. Within each organ set, cDNA was normalized, and 13–20 PCR cycles were run depending on cDNA amount. The average fragment length of 10x cDNA libraries was quantified on a Fragment Analyzer (AATI) and by qPCR using the Kapa Library Quantification Kit for Illumina. Each library was diluted to 4 nM, and equal volumes were pooled for each sequencing run.     Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using 100-cycle run kits, with 28 bases for Read 1, 8 bases for Index 1, and 91 bases for Read 2 (Illumina 20012862). A PhiX control library was spiked in at 0.2–1%.     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.
_source.Study Description: Spaceflights significantly impacts astronaut health, causing muscle atrophy, bone loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and immune system dysregulation, especially during long missions. To explore molecular changes, we generated a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset, of 216 samples from 28 mouse organs and tissues under spaceflight and control conditions. Since spaceflight effects closely resemble aspects of aging, we included two age groups (3 and 8 months) to assess age-related influences. Our data revealed that spaceflight drives age-independent systemic changes, primarily affecting tissue remodeling and alterations in cytoskeleton, membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly in endothelial cells. In contrast, aging has a weaker impact, mainly altering immune regulation in an age-dependent manner. These findings suggest that cytoskeletal and ECM changes may contribute to immune Dysregulation.

_source.Study Protocol Description: Donor and muscle biopsy data analysis: Cells from the same lot of muscle biopsy cells used for our SpaceX CRS-21 mission (Parafati et al., 2023) were subsequently purified and seeded for the SpaceX CRS-25 mission and represented independent experiments. In brief, percutaneous biopsies were obtained from the middle region of the vastus lateralis using a Bergstrom needle (as previously described, Sparks et al., 2011), from five young, active male volunteers (mean 35 +/- 4) and five old, sedentary male volunteers (mean 70 +/- 4). Participants were considered active if they engaged in endurance exercise at least 3 days a week without extensive lay off over the previous 6 months. Participants were considered sedentary if they completed one or fewer structured exercise sessions a week. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the institutional review board at AdventHealth, Orlando (IRBNet  554559). Myoblast purification: Harvested cells were purified with an immuno-magnetic sorting system (Miltenyi Biotec, Paris, France) using an anti-CD56/NCAM antibody as described (Giza et al., 2022). Purified myoblasts were plated in collagen-coated Petri dishes and cultured in skeletal muscle cell growth medium (PromoCell Cat  C-23060) supplemented with 0.1 mg/mL primosin to protect cultures from microbial contamination, 5% fetal bovine serum, and gentamicin at 37C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2. At cell isolation, all human myoblasts were at passage 4 and expanded to passage 6. Passage numbers were matched for young- and old-derived donor cells. Myoblasts from different donors were pooled in a 1:1 ratio, and aliquots were cryopreserved. Enrichment was confirmed by comparing CD56− and CD56+ cell populations by fluorescence-activated cell sorting staining as described (Giza et al., 2022).     Donor-derived 3D myobundles were generated by seeding myoblasts in tissue-engineered constructs and launched to the ISS aboard the SpaceX CRS-25 commercial resupply mission. Cell seeding was performed at NASA’s Kennedy Space Station Processing Facility (SSPF) for flight and asynchronously at the University of Florida laboratory for the ground test. CD56+-enriched myoblasts were mixed in a collagen-Matrigel hydrogel and injected into the PDMS-based chips at a final cell density of 15 and 20 million cells/mL, for YA and OS-derived cell stocks, respectively, and allowed to polymerize at 37C for 60 min as previously described (Giza et al., 2022; Parafati et al., 2023). Differentiation followed a two-step process as previously described (Giza et al., 2022; Parafati et al., 2023, 2025). Sixteen tissue chips were integrated onto the CubeLab manifold on day 8 of growth, and media for flight was stored at 6C–8C in a gas-permeable bag. On day 14, 30 min of E-Stim of 3 V, 2 Hz, 2-ms pulse was applied sequentially to four YA and four OS tissue chips; the other eight chips were No E-Stim. Donor-derived 3D myobundles were maintained in the Space Tango CubeLab at 37C and 5%–6% CO2 for both the flight and ground payloads. The myobundles were cultured in maintenance medium that was changed every 6 h to maintain healthy muscle microtissues.     We performed transcript profiling of YA- and OS-derived myoblasts cultured for 2 and 21 days (including 12 days of spaceflight) and compared them with myoblasts grown on ground for the full 21 days by RNA-seq. Cultures in tissue chip devices were preserved with RNAlater (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and frozen at −20C to −30C.     Cells were lysed in the chip, and RNA isolation was performed using RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (QIAGEN) as previously described (Parafati et al., 2023). RNA concentration and quality were determined with Agilent TapeStation 2200 (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). 500 ng of total RNA was used for RNA sample preparation and processed in triplicate for a total of 30 samples.     Strand-specific RNA-seq libraries were generated using the NEBNext Ultra Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA) as previously described (Parafati et al., 2023). First, 100 ng of total RNA was used for mRNA isolated using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (New England Biolabs, catalog   E7490). Then followed by RNA library construction with the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, catalog  E7760) according to the manufacturer's user guide. Briefly, RNA was fragmented in NEBNext First Strand Synthesis Buffer via incubation at 94 C for the desired time. This step was followed by first-strand cDNA synthesis using reverse transcriptase and random hexamer primer. Synthesis of ds-cDNA was performed using the 2nd strand master mix provided in the kit, followed by end-repair and adaptor ligation. At this point, Illumina adaptors were ligated to the sample. Finally, each library (uniquely barcoded) was enriched by 12 cycles of amplification, and purified with Agencourt AMPure beads (Beckman Coulter, catalog   A63881). 15 barcoded libraries were sized on the TapeStation 4200 and quantified with the Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer.     Barcoded libraries were pooled equimolarly for sequencing simultaneously for Illumina NovaSeq X. Sequencing and bioinformatics were performed at the University of Florida Interdisciplinary Center for Biotechnology Research core facility.     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.12.1 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.26. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of H-sapiens rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.     Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Homo Sapiens STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCh38 (Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa) and the following gtf annotation file: Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.112.gtf. Trimmed reads were aligned to the Homo Sapiens STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to reverse and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0) and normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Hs.eg.db (version 3.19.1).

_source.Study Publication Title: Microgravity accelerates skeletal muscle degeneration: Functional and transcriptomic insights from an ISS muscle lab-on-chip model.
_source.Study Description: Microgravity accelerates skeletal muscle degeneration, mimicking aspects of aging, yet its effects on muscle cell function remain underexplored. Using a muscle lab-on-chip model onboard the International Space Station (ISS), we examined 3D-bioengineered myobundles derived from young and older adult donors under microgravity. Electrical stimulation applied intermittently to the myobundles revealed reduced contraction magnitude in microgravity and decreased protein levels of myosin heavy chain 7, a main isoform in slow-twitch muscle fibers. Transcriptomic profiling revealed active myogenesis across ground and spaceflight samples, but younger electrically stimulated myobundles displayed enhanced mitochondrial-related gene expression in microgravity, while older and non-electrically stimulated myobundles were less responsive. Comparative analysis between young and older derived myobundles identified 86 muscle-specific age-associated genes altered in microgravity, linked to inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cellular stress. These findings highlight a unique age-related molecular response in microgravity and underscores electrical stimulation as a potential countermeasure. These insights advance our understanding of muscle aging and degeneration in microgravity, guiding future therapeutic strategies.

_source.Study Protocol Description:
The 16-week-old female C57 BL/6J mice (Jackson Lab, Bar Harbor, ME) were used in this study as part of the NASA RR-1 project consortium. This project was approved by the NASA Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Both spaceflight and ground control animals were housed in NASA’s animal enclosure modules (AEM), with control mice being exposed to the same environment conditions (12-hour light cycle, temperature and humidity) as those flown on the International Space Station (ISS). Control animals were kept inside an environmental simulator (ISSES) at the Space Life Science Laboratory (SLSL) at Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and the spaceflight animals were transported to the ISS by SpaceX4 on September 21, 2014. All animals were fed with a special NASA food bar diet and their health was checked daily. The spaceflight mice were euthanized and frozen on-orbit after 37 days of flight, while ground control mice were simultaneously euthanized and frozen under identical conditions.     After the frozen carcasses were returned to KSC, the ocular tissues were removed from both groups. At the time of dissections, both eyes were dissected from the carcasses thawed at room temperature for 15 - 20 minutes. The eyes were harvested and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, then stored at −80C. The frozen whole eye samples were micro-dissected in the ice-cold phosphate buffered saline (PBS). Fine spring scissors were used to separate the cornea from the sclera to access the retina. The retina was carefully detached from the sclera. The retina, cornea, and lens were immediately frozen on dry ice and stored at −80C before DNA and RNA isolations.     Retinal tissues (4 -20 mg) were homogenized with Precellys CKM beads (Hilden, Germany) in 350 ul of Qiagen RLT plus buffer. The genomic DNA (gDNA) and total RNA were isolated using the Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA/miRNA Universal Kit according to the manufacturer's protocol. After isolation, RNA and DNA were frozen and kept at -80 C until further use. Isolated RNA samples were quantified using NanoDrop spectrophotometry (Thermo Scientific, Chino, CA). DNA and RNA were further quantified using the Qubit dsDNA High Sensitivity Kit and RNA Broad Range Kit, respectively (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA). RNA quality was evaluated using the Agilent 2200 TapeStation and RNA ScreenTape (Santa Clara, CA). All RNA samples had an integrity numbers (RIN) ranging from 7.2 to 8.1.     The Ovation Mouse RNA-Seq System 1 - 16 (NuGEN Technologies, San Carlos, CA) was used to construct RNA-seq libraries according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, 100 ng of total RNA spiked with 1 ul of 1:500 diluted ERCC Mix 1 (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA) was used to start cDNA synthesis. Following the primer annealing and cDNA synthesis, the products (130 ul/each sample) were sheared using Covaris S220 Focused-ultrasonicator (Covaris Inc., Woburn, MA). The parameters were set as follows: 10% duty factor, peak power 175 and 200 cycles per burst at 4 C for 200 seconds to obtain fragment sizes between 150 - 200 bp. The products were then subject to end-repair, adaptor index ligation and strand selection. A custom InDA-C primer mixture SS5 Version 5 for mouse was used to allow strand selection. Finally, the libraries were amplified on a PCR thermocycler for 17 cycles (MastercyclerR pro, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany), and purified with RNAClean XP Agencourt beads (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN); and quantified using Qubit dsDNA HS Kit on Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA). The quality and peak size were determined using the D1000 ScreenTape on Agilent 2200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA).

One hundred (100) ng of gDNA was used to construct RRBS DNA-seq library using the Ovation RRBS Methyl-Seq System (NuGEN Technologies, San Carlos, CA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, the MspI enzyme, which cuts the DNA at CCGG sites, was used to digest gDNA into fragments. The fragments were directly subject to end blunting and phosphorylation in preparation for ligation to a methylated adapter with a single-base T overhang. A unique index, out of 16 indices, was used for each individual sample for multiplexing. The ligation products were repaired in a thermal cycler under the program (60 C -10 min, 70 C -10 min, hold at 4 C). The products of the final repair reaction were used for bisulfite conversion using QIAGEN EpiTect Fast DNA Bisulfite Kit according to Qiagen's protocol. Bisulfiteconverted DNA was then amplified (MastercyclerR pro, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany), and bead-purified with Agencourt RNAClean XP beads.     The RRBS libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 550, 75 bp, single-end read, whereas the RNAseq libraries were sequenced on both Illumina NextSeq 550 and HiSeq 4000, pair-end reads (76 bpx2), at the Loma Linda University (LLU) Center for Genomics.     Raw fastq files from each sample were assessed for % rRNA using HTStream SeqScreener (version 1.3.2) screened against a fasta file of Mus musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 01-Sep-2021. Raw fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1) and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports.     Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.1.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_RNASeq_Workflow/tree/NF_RCP_2.1.0). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0), ERCC genes were removed, and the non-ERCC genes were normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1). Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.

_source.Study Funding Agency: This work was supported by the NSF/CASIS (CBET 2126309) and NASA (80JSC018M0005) grants to A.R. Muotri. Additional support was provided by the Alzheimer's Association (AARF-25-1473595), CAPES (Finance Code 001), and CNPq (grants 311438/2022-9 and 402773/2022-5).
_source.Study Protocol Description:
Four human iPSC lines were used: a healthy control line (7889SA; New York Stem Cell Foundation) and three isogenic lines carrying heterozygous CRISPR-engineered mutations in PSEN1 (WT/M233L), PSEN2 (WT/N141I), and APP (WT/V717G). The PSEN1 and APP lines had been generated previously, and the PSEN2 mutation was introduced into the control background by Synthego Engineered Cells. iPSCs were maintained on Matrigel-coated plates (Corning) in mTeSR1 medium (StemCell Technologies) with daily media changes.

On day 0 of differentiation, iPSCs were dissociated with StemPro Accutase (Thermo Fisher Scientific,  A1110501), centrifuged (4 min, 200 × g), and resuspended in mTeSR1 supplemented with 10 uM Y-27632 ROCK inhibitor (Selleck Chemicals), 10 uM SB431542 (Stemgent,  04-0010), and 1 uM Dorsomorphin (RandD Systems,  3093). Approximately 2.5 × 10^6 single cells were seeded per well of a 6-well ultra-low attachment plate (Corning) and kept under continuous orbital rotation (95 rpm). Cortical specification followed a semi-guided differentiation protocol.

Neural induction (days 3–9): On day 3, mTeSR1 was replaced with Media 1: Neurobasal Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific,  21103049) containing 1× GlutaMAX, 1% N2 supplement, 2% Gem21 NeuroPlex (GeminiBio), 1% MEM Non-Essential Amino Acids, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, 10 uM SB431542, and 1 uM Dorsomorphin. Organoids were cultured in Media 1 for 6 days, with media changes every other day.

NPC proliferation (days 9–22): On day 9, cultures were transferred to Media 2: Neurobasal with 1× GlutaMAX, 2% Gem21 NeuroPlex, 1% NEAA, and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, supplemented with 20 ng/mL bFGF (PeproTech). Media was exchanged daily for 7 days. From days 16–22, organoids were kept in Media 2 with both 20 ng/mL bFGF and 20 ng/mL EGF (PeproTech), with media changes every other day.

Neuronal differentiation (days 22–28): On day 22, organoids were switched to Media 3: Media 2 supplemented with 10 ng/mL BDNF, 10 ng/mL GDNF, 10 ng/mL NT-3 (all PeproTech), 200 μM L-ascorbic acid, and 1 mM dibutyryl-cAMP (both Sigma-Aldrich). Media was refreshed every other day for 6 days. From day 28 onward, organoids were kept in Media 2, with media exchanges every 3–4 days.

Quality control: All organoid cultures were routinely tested for mycoplasma by PCR on media supernatants, and only negative cultures were used. After differentiation, the diameter of every organoid was measured using GelCount (Oxford Optronix), and cortical identity was confirmed by immunofluorescence (MAP2, SOX2) on 30-day-old organoids.     Cortical organoids were generated from four human iPSC lines: a healthy control line (7889SA) and three isogenic lines carrying heterozygous CRISPR-engineered familial Alzheimer’s disease mutations, PSEN1 (WT/M233L), PSEN2 (WT/N141I), and APP (WT/V717G). At one month of age, organoids of each genotype (Control, APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) were prepared for spaceflight, with twelve independent organoids per genotype × environment combination. Organoids were transferred to cryovials (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
 374088) containing ~2 mL of Media 2 (Neurobasal Medium with 1× GlutaMAX, 2% Gem21 NeuroPlex, 1% NEAA, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin, and 20 ng/mL bFGF). Loaded cryovials were hand-carried from UC San Diego to NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and placed into a High Sample Capacity CubeLab (Space Tango Inc.), an autonomous incubator that maintained 37C and 5% CO2 throughout the mission. The flight CubeLab was integrated into the SpaceX Dragon capsule and launched to the ISS on the SpaceX CRS-30 mission on March 21, 2024. It returned to Earth on April 30, 2024. Ground control organoids were kept in a matching CubeLab at KSC labs under identical conditions: the same sealed cryovial system, CubeLab hardware, media volume, culture duration, temperature, CO2 control, and handling procedures.     Following splashdown on April 30, 2024, the CubeLab payload was returned to NASA's Space Station Processing Facility (SSPF), where it was opened and the organoid samples were retrieved during de-integration on the same day. The samples were immediately frozen on dry ice and subsequently stored at −80°C until further processing. For RNA sequencing, individual organoids were harvested as separate samples, and total RNA was extracted from each organoid independently. A total of 46 organoid samples were included in the final RNA-seq dataset: Control (Ground n equals 6, ISS n equals 6), APP (Ground n equals 6, ISS n equals 6), PSEN1 (Ground n equals 4, ISS n equals 6), and PSEN2 (Ground n equals 6, ISS n equals 6). One PSEN1 Ground sample was excluded due to poor RNA quality (RIN 2.6). To maintain consistency and avoid including an incomplete biological replicate, we excluded both experimental replicates associated with that biological sample. Therefore, the final dataset contains four samples representing two independent biological replicates (n equals 4).     Total RNA was extracted from individual cortical organoids using the RNeasy Plus Micro Kit Qiagen according to the manufacturer instructions. Organoids were lysed and homogenized, and genomic DNA was removed using gDNA eliminator columns included in the kit. RNA was purified through silica membrane spin columns and eluted in RNase free water. RNA concentration was measured using a Qubit fluorometric assay and RNA integrity was assessed using an Agilent Tapestation system. Only samples with RNA integrity number greater than 8 were used for downstream library preparation. For RNA sequencing n 3 biological replicates per genotype per condition total n 23 samples were processed.     RNA sequencing libraries were prepared from high quality total RNA using the Illumina Stranded mRNA Prep kit according to the manufacturer instructions. Briefly polyadenylated RNA was enriched from total RNA and fragmented followed by first strand cDNA synthesis and second strand synthesis to generate double stranded cDNA. End repair and adapter ligation were performed and libraries were amplified by PCR. Library quality and concentration were assessed prior to sequencing. For RNA sequencing, n equals 3 biological replicates (individual organoids) per genotype per condition were used. Two independent technical-duplicate libraries were prepared from each RNA sample (48 libraries in total) and sequenced on separate lanes (L005 and L006) of the same NovaSeq 6000 run. One PSEN1 Ground biological replicate (GROUND_PSEN1_C) was excluded due to low RNA quality (RIN equals 2.6), and both of its libraries were removed, resulting in 46 libraries from 23 biological replicates in the final dataset.     RNA sequencing libraries were multiplexed and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using paired end reads of 151 base pairs. Sequencing was performed to achieve an average depth of approximately 25 million reads per sample. Base calling and demultiplexing were carried out using Illumina bcl2fastq software to generate FASTQ files for downstream analysis. Two independent technical-duplicate libraries were prepared from each RNA sample (48 libraries in total) and sequenced on separate lanes (L005 and L006) of the same NovaSeq 6000 run. One PSEN1 Ground biological replicate (GROUND_PSEN1_C) was excluded due to low RNA quality (RIN equals 2.6), and both of its libraries were removed, resulting in 46 libraries from 23 biological replicates in the final dataset.     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.4.1 screened against a fasta file of H-sapiens rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 08-Jan-2026.

_source.Study Publication Title: Spaceflight accelerates Alzheimer’s disease–associated molecular programs in human brain organoids
_source.Study Description: Spaceflight provides a unique environment to study neural responses relevant to neurodegenerative diseases. Here, human cortical organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that carry familial Alzheimer's disease (fAD) mutations in APP (p.V717G), PSEN1 (p.M233L), and PSEN2 (p.N141I) were cultivated at the International Space Station (ISS) alongside isogenic controls for 40 days. Multi-omic profiling, integrating transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolic analyses, revealed a coordinated shift in neuronal and cellular states during spaceflight. AD-derived organoids showed altered glycolytic activity and altered lactate-to-malate ratios, consistent with metabolic and mitochondrial remodeling. Spaceflight was also associated with changes in amyloid-beta (AB) processing and tau phosphorylation, although the magnitude and direction of these responses varied across genetic backgrounds. Pathway analysis identified increased synaptic and neurotransmission-related signatures, particularly those associated with GABAergic and glutamatergic signaling. Integrative analysis further revealed convergent programs involving RNA processing, chromatin organization, cytoskeletal dynamics, and cellular stress responses. Proteomic and multi-omic analyses also identified changes in RNA-binding proteins, including CIRBP, consistent with altered post-transcriptional regulatory networks under spaceflight conditions. Collectively, these exploratory findings indicate that spaceflight reshapes neuronal and metabolic regulation in human brain organoids, revealing coordinated molecular responses relevant to AD biology.

_source.Study Protocol Description: Twenty (20) mice (male, C57BL/6J, 16-17 weeks old) were launched in one Transporter on SpaceX-21 (SpX-21) on December 6, 2020. The Flight mice were transferred into two Rodent Habitats upon arrival to the International Space Station (ISS) and were maintained in microgravity for 38 days. The Flight mice were transferred into a Transporter and returned to Earth for Live Animal Return (LAR) on SpX-21 (January 13th, 2021). After Atlantic Ocean splashdown, the LAR Flight mice were transported via helicopter to Kennedy Space Center. Collectively, 20 Flight, 20 HGC, and 20 VGC mice were transferred from Rodent Transporters (Flight and HGC) or vivarium cages (VGC) and placed into shipping containers. All 60 mice were flown via charter plane to the PI’s institution, Texas A and M University (TAMU). The study followed recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and the protocol (Protocol number RR-23) was approved by the NASA Flight Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).     All post-flight euthanasia and dissections were performed by the PI team at TAMU. The original plan was to perform all pre-flight and post-flight activities at Roskamp Institute in Sarasota, Florida.  Due to the health risks associated with travel during the COVID-19 pandemic, HRP approved all post-flight activities at TAMU, which significantly decreased or eliminated travel for the PI, BSP, and Payload Developer (PD) teams. Upon arrival at the TAMU Animal Care Facility (ACF), the mice underwent post-flight procedures, followed by euthanasia and tissue collection by the PI team. GeneLab only processed 9/9/9 samples from Flight/HGC/VGC groups in this dataset.     RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Universal Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD). Approximately 20mg of tissue was used, weighed, and immediately placed in 800 uL of the QIAzol buffer solution. Homogenization was performed using tissue homogenizing bead mix SSB14B, a mix of stainless steel beads of 0.9-2mm (Next Advance, Raymertown, NY) on Bullet Blender Gold 24 (Next Advance, Raymertown, NY) for 5 minutes at 4oC, speed of 12 per SOP 2.1-Tissue homogenization Using Bullet Blender Gold Bead Beater. Homogenates were centrifuged for 5 minutes at RT and 14,000 g to remove cell debris. The supernatant from each sample was then used to isolate and purify RNA following the manufacturer protocol. RNA was eluted in 30 uL RNAse free H2O. Concentration for all RNA samples were measured using Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) with Qubit RNA BR kit following SOP 4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. RNA quality was assessed using the Agilent 4200 TapeStation with the Agilent RNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     ERCC ExFold RNA Spike-In Mixes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, Cat 4456739, v92), Mix 1 or Mix 2, were added on the day of library prep at the concentrations suggested by the manufacturer protocol. Following SOP 5.2 Use of ERCC Spike-In Mixes and UMRR/UHRR Controls for Total RNA Sequencing. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     RNA ribo depletion and library preparation was done with Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Gold (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA). Input RNA were approximately 500 ng with RIN less than 7.4. Index adapters used were at 1.5 uM (IDT, 384-well xGen Dual Index UMI Adapters). 15 cycles PCR were performed. Library fragment size was assessed using Agilent 4200 TapeStation with D1000 DNA ScreenTape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) following GeneLab SOP 6.3 Quality analysis of sequencing libraries using 4200 TapeStation System with D1000 reagent kit. Pooled library concentration was measured by Qubit 4 Fluorometer (ThermoFisher Scentific, Waltham, MA) following SOP 4.1-RNA/DNA/miRNA/cDNA Quantification using Qubit Fluorimeter. Library quality assessment was performed on iSeq100 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). Two separate libraries were made from the same extracted RNA pool for samples RR23_R-Quad_FLT_F1 and RR23_R-Quad_GC_G1, to give technical replicates 1 and 2 for each sample. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     RNA sequencing was performed by GeneLab Sample Processing Lab on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Sequencing was set up as following: Read 1: 151bp, Index1: 17bp, Index2: 8bp Read 2:151bp. PhiX included as control and to increase library diversity. Protocol followed is SOP 7.1-Setting up NovaSeq 6000 and iSeq 100 Sequencers. GeneLab Sample Processing SOP can be found at the GitHub page, https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab-sampleProcessing/tree/master/SOP_docs.     Raw fastq files from each sample were assessed for % rRNA using HTStream SeqScreener (version 1.3.2) screened against a fasta file of Mus musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on Sep-2021. Raw fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1) and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports.     Data were processed as described in GL-DPPD-7101-G (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/master/RNAseq/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7101_Versions/GL-DPPD-7101-G.md), using NF_RCP version 2.0.0 (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/tree/NF_RCP_2.0.0/RNAseq/Workflow_Documentation/NF_RCP). In short, raw fastq files were filtered using Trim Galore! (version 0.6.10) powered by Cutadapt (version 4.2). Trimmed fastq file quality was evaluated with FastQC (version 0.12.1), and MultiQC (version 1.26) was used to generate MultiQC reports. Mus Musculus STAR and RSEM references were built using STAR (version 2.7.11b) and RSEM (version 1.3.3), respectively, Ensembl release 112, genome assembly GRCm39 (Mus_musculus.GRCm39.dna.primary_assembly.fa) concatenated with ERCC92.fa from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip), and the following gtf annotation file: Mus_musculus.GRCm39.112.gtf concatenated with the ERCC92.gtf file from ThermoFisher (https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LSG/manuals/ERCC92.zip). Trimmed reads were aligned to the Mus Musculus + ERCC STAR reference with STAR (version 2.7.11b) and alignment log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). Aligned reads were assessed for strandedness using RSeQC infer_experiment.py (version 5.0.4), gene body coverage using RSeQC geneBody_coverage.py (version 5.0.4), inner distance was assessed using RSeQC inner_distance.py (version 5.0.4), and distribution of RNA features using RSeQC read_distribution.py (version 5.0.4). Aligned reads from all samples were quantified using RSEM (version 1.3.3), with strandedness set to forward and RSEM count log files were compiled with MultiQC (version 1.26). To create a set of rRNA-removed quantification data, Ensembl IDs mapping to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) were removed from the RSEM gene count data. Both the original set of RSEM quantification data and the rRNA-removed data were subject to differential gene expression analysis as follows. A runsheet was generated with dp_tools (version 1.3.8) and the runsheet and quantification data were imported to R (version 4.4.2) with tximport (version 1.34.0), ERCC genes were removed, and the non-ERCC genes were normalized with DESeq2 (version 1.46.0) median of ratios method. Normalized gene counts were subject to differential expression analysis. For samples with technical replicates, only the first replicate was used for count normalization and differential expression analysis. Differential expression analysis was performed in R (version 4.4.2) using DESeq2 (version 1.46.0); all groups were compared pairwise using the Wald test and the likelihood ratio test was used to generate the F statistic p-value. Gene annotations were assigned using the custom annotation tables generated in-house as detailed in GL-DPPD-7110-A (https://github.com/nasa/GeneLab_Data_Processing/blob/GL_RefAnnotTable-A_1.1.0/GeneLab_Reference_Annotations/Pipeline_GL-DPPD-7110_Versions/GL-DPPD-7110-A/GL-DPPD-7110-A.md), with STRINGdb (version 2.16.4), PANTHER.db (version 1.0.12), and org.Mm.eg.db (version 3.19.1). Assessment of ERCC spiked genes was performed as detailed in the ERCC_analysis_GLbulkRNAseq.html report.
_source.Study Description: The objective of the Rodent Research-23 mission (RR-23) was to better understand the effects of spaceflight on the eyes, specifically on the structure and function of the arteries, veins, and lymphatic vessels that are needed to maintain vision. To this end, twenty male, C57BL/6J, 16-17 weeks-old mice were delivered to the International Space Station (ISS) on SpaceX-21 in a single transporter, transferred to two rodent habitats, and maintained in microgravity for 38 days. Flight mice were then returned to Earth alive (January 13th, 2021). After splashdown in the Atlantic Ocean, mice were transported to Kennedy Space Center via helicopter. The 20 Flight, 20 Habitat Ground Control (HGC), and 20 Vivarium Ground Control (VGC) mice were removed from Rodent Transporters (Flight and HGC) or vivarium cages (VGC), placed into shipping containers, and flown to Texas A and M University. There, mice underwent post-flight procedures, before euthanasia and tissue collection. Flight, HGC and VGC animals were euthanized and dissected on Jan 14th, 17th or 20th of 2021, respectively. Right quadriceps femoris muscle samples were preserved by immersion in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80C until RNA was extracted, and libraries generated and sequenced (target 60 M clusters per sample, PE 150 bp). This dataset features 9 samples from the Flight group, 9 samples from the Habitat Ground Control group, and 9 samples from the Vivarium Ground Control group.

The quality of libraries was assessed using Agilent TapeStation 4200, and test-sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 550.     The full sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 by SeqMatic (Fremont, CA).     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. De-identified peripheral blood buffy coat samples were obtained from healthy human donors from the Stanford University Blood Center. PBMCs were isolated using a Ficoll gradient method. To generate simulated microgravity, the cell suspension was loaded into 10 ml disposable high aspect ratio vessels (Synthecon, Houston, TX) and rotated at 15 rpm for 25 hours.
For the 1G control, the cell suspension was plated in standard 6-well culture plates, as standard static culture plates or culture flasks have been shown to be comparable to static high aspect ratio vessels by others in major immunological assays. 1G and simulated microgravity cultures were simultaneously placed in the same 37 C, 5% CO2 incubator. To stimulate PBMCs, samples were mixed with 1 μM R848 (TLR7/8 agonist, Invivogen, San Diego, CA) after 16 hours, for 9 hours of stimulation. _source.Study Publication Title: Single-cell analysis identifies conserved features of immune dysfunction in simulated microgravity and spaceflight
_source.Study Description: Microgravity is associated with immunological dysfunction, though the mechanisms are poorly understood. Here, using single-cell analysis of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) exposed to short term (25 hours) simulated microgravity, we characterize altered genes and pathways at basal and stimulated states with a Toll-like Receptor-7/8 agonist. We validate single-cell analysis by RNA sequencing and super-resolution microscopy, and against data from the Inspiration-4 (I4) mission, JAXA (Cell-Free Epigenome) mission, Twins study, and spleens from mice on the International Space Station. Overall, microgravity alters specific pathways for optimal immunity, including the cytoskeleton, interferon signaling, pyroptosis, temperature-shock, innate inflammation (e.g., Coronavirus pathogenesis pathway and IL-6 signaling), nuclear receptors, and sirtuin signaling. Microgravity directs monocyte inflammatory parameters, and impairs T cell and NK cell functionality. Using machine learning, we identify numerous compounds linking microgravity to immune cell transcription, and demonstrate that the flavonol, quercetin, can reverse most abnormal pathways. These results define immune cell alterations in microgravity, and provide opportunities for countermeasures to maintain normal immunity in space.
